questions.stem: Which multiplication has the same answer as 10 + 10?
questions.stemText: Which multiplication has the same answer as 10 + 10 ?
questions.explain: Count the 10s: there are 2 of them, so this is 2 groups of 10, which is 2 × 10 = 20. Counting one group too many gives 3 × 10, which is 10 too much, and multiplying the wrong pair gives 10 × 10 or 3 × 2. Multiplication is a short way of writing the same number added over and over - that is the whole idea, and it is why the times tables are worth knowing by heart.

questions.stem: Priya works out 2334 + 1192 in columns. One column makes 12, so she writes 2 in that column and a small 1 above the column on its left. How much is that small 1 worth?
questions.stemText: Priya works out 2334 + 1192 in columns. One column makes 12, so she writes 2 in that column and a small 1 above the column on its left. How much is that small 1 worth?
questions.explain: The column that makes 12 is the tens column: 3 + 9 = 12, and no other column reaches ten. 12 tens is 1 hundred and 2 tens, so the 2 stays in the tens column - worth 20 - and the small 1 goes above the hundreds column - worth 100. The small 1 is worth 100. A mark is worth the column it is written in, not the digit it looks like: that is what regrouping means, ten of something small becoming one of the next size up. Every wrong answer here is one of the two slips - the right digit read in the wrong column, or the wrong digit read in the right one.

questions.stem: Mei Ling works out 81 + 82 in her head. She makes 90 first. 81 + 82 = 90 + ?
questions.stemText: Mei Ling works out 81 + 82 in her head. She makes 90 first. 81 + 82 = 90 + ?
questions.explain: To get from 81 up to 90 you need 9, so 9 is moved across from the 82. That leaves 82 − 9 = 73, and 90 + 73 = 163. Whatever you give to one number you must take off the other, or the total changes. You could have rounded the 82 up to 90 instead and taken that amount off the 81: it is the same total either way, so it lands on the same answer.
